opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly I think it's one of the most underrated open problems right now.

When people talk about research taste, they usually mean knowing which problems are worth working on, which directions are likely to pan out, and when to abandon something that isn't working. For human researchers, that mostly comes from experience. You try a lot of things, most of them fail, and over time you build an intuition for what tends to work. You also absorb it from mentors and colleagues.

I think models will improve along a similar path. The key ingredient is feedback on long-horizon outcomes. Right now we're very good at training models on tasks where you get a clear signal quickly: did the code pass the tests, did you get the math problem right? Research taste is harder because the feedback is delayed and noisy. You might pick a direction, and you won't know for weeks or months whether it was a good call. Even then, it's hard to attribute success or failure to the original decision.

As models become capable of running longer experiments more autonomously, they'll get many more of those feedback loops. A human researcher might get a few dozen meaningful "this direction worked" or "this didn't" signals in a career. A model that runs many experiments in parallel could potentially get far more. That's a real advantage.

I'd also be a bit cautious. Taste isn't just pattern-matching on what worked before. Some of the most important research comes from going against the consensus and pursuing something that looks unpromising. Before the reasoning paradigm took off, many people thought scaling test-time compute wasn't the right bet. So you want models that can learn from history without just converging on whatever's fashionable.

My guess is that we'll see models first become very useful as research assistants, running experiments and surfacing results, and taste will improve gradually as they get more of that long-horizon feedback. I don't think there's a single breakthrough moment. It'll be a steady progression, and at some point we'll look back and realize the models' judgment is genuinely good.

r001.rationale: The response describes research taste improving gradually through long-horizon feedback and explicitly says there will not be a single breakthrough moment. It does not suggest a sudden inflection point to usefulness.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think research taste is one of these things that people treat as kind of mystical, like it's this innate quality that some researchers have and others don't. And I don't really buy that. I think research taste is mostly the result of experience. It's the result of having tried a lot of things, seen what works and what doesn't, and building up an intuition for which directions are promising and which are dead ends.

And the reason I'm optimistic that models will get better at this is that it's fundamentally a learnable skill. When I think about how I developed taste, it was by running experiments, being wrong a lot, and slowly updating. It's a feedback loop. And models can go through that feedback loop much faster than humans can. They can run more experiments, they can look at more results, and if you set up the training correctly, they can learn from the outcomes of those experiments.

Right now, I think the models are actually pretty good at the execution side of research. If you tell them exactly what to do, they can implement it, they can debug it, they can run it. Where they're weaker is in deciding what's worth doing in the first place. What's the question that, if you answered it, would actually move things forward? That's the part that still requires a lot of human judgment.

But I think that gap closes for the same reason the reasoning gap closed. A few years ago people said models can't really reason, they just pattern match. And then we found that if you train them with the right objectives, with reinforcement learning on tasks where you can verify outcomes, they get a lot better at reasoning. I think research is similar. Research has a reward signal. Did the experiment work? Did the idea pan out? Did it lead somewhere? It's a noisier and longer-horizon signal than something like math, but it's there.

So my view is that it's less about some fundamental limitation and more about the fact that we haven't yet built the right environments and training loops for it. And once we do, I'd expect taste to improve the way everything else has improved, which is to say faster than people expect.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that research taste will improve through training and feedback, but does not suggest it will suddenly reach an inflection point where it becomes useful.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it will come from closing the loop between having an idea and finding out whether it works. Research taste is partly being able to predict which experiments are worth running, and you develop that by running experiments and being surprised by the results.

If a model is only trained to produce a plausible research proposal, that's a different objective from producing an idea that actually leads to a useful discovery. Once models can carry out experiments, interpret the results, and use that feedback to choose what to try next, I think their taste will improve.

The challenging part is the time horizon. An idea might look unpromising after a day but turn out to be valuable after a month. You want models that can pursue those ideas without just continuing indefinitely on something that isn't working. That's a harder capability to train and evaluate than solving a problem where you can immediately check the answer.

r001.rationale: The response says research taste may improve through experiments and feedback, but it does not suggest a sudden inflection point where it becomes useful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of research taste comes from actually doing research and seeing what works. You have an idea that seems promising, you run the experiment, and then you find out that your intuition was wrong. Over time, that feedback helps you choose better problems and better approaches.

Models today learn a lot from the finished products of research—papers, code—but those don’t capture all the failed experiments and decisions that went into them. So I’d expect a big improvement as models get to participate in that process themselves: propose ideas, test them, and learn from the outcomes.

The hard part is that the feedback can take a long time. An idea might look unpromising initially and turn out to be important. So you want models that can make good bets, but also pursue something long enough to learn whether it actually works.

r001.rationale: The response predicts research taste will improve through participation and feedback, but it does not suggest that the improvement will reach a sudden inflection point or become useful then.
